title: Tokyo Was Once Called Edo
visual_style: photographic travel documentary; archival assets only when license-verified; no character assets
script: Tokyo was once known by another name: Edo.
Its rise accelerated when Tokugawa Ieyasu established his government here in 1603.
Edo became a political and cultural center under the Tokugawa shogunate.
By the eighteenth century, it had grown into a vast metropolis.
For centuries, the emperor's court remained in Kyoto.
Then 1868 brought a turning point in Japanese history.
Edo was renamed Tokyo, meaning eastern capital.
The city changed, but traces of Edo survived.
Look for them in historic districts, gardens, and museums.
Nihonbashi became a key bridge and commercial center.
Its old routes connected Edo with places across Japan.
The city also developed distinctive theatre, prints, and festivals.
Modern streets now sit beside older cultural landmarks.
A museum can help put those layers into context.
For a visit, choose one historic district and walk slowly.
Check official site information before planning museum entry.
